candidate.topic: Why ankle flexibility predicts squat depth more than hip mobility
candidate.hook: Your hips aren’t the gatekeeper of squat depth—your ankles are. Knee-over-toe range (ankle dorsiflexion) predicts how deep you can squat far better than hip mobility does.
candidate.frame: We’re looking at squat depth through your ankles—how much knee-over-toe dorsiflexion you own—not through how open your hips feel. Use that lens and the cues and fixes that follow will make sense.
candidate.payload:
Ankle dorsiflexion is the bottleneck for most people’s squat depth because it determines how far your knees can travel over your toes to keep your center of mass over mid‑foot; when dorsiflexion is limited, you either pitch your torso forward, lift your heels, or stop early regardless of how “open” your hips feel (per Macrum et al. 2012). In controlled trials, restricting dorsiflexion reduces squat depth and increases trunk lean and hip flexion, while elevating the heel with weightlifting shoes increases tibial inclination and enables deeper positions with a more upright torso (per Macrum et al. 2012; Sato et al. 2012). The weight‑bearing lunge (knee‑to‑wall) test is a reliable way to quantify your usable dorsiflexion and is a practical screen to predict who will struggle to hit depth without compensations (per Bennell et al. 1998). Hips still matter for stance and comfort, but if your knee‑to‑wall is limited or asymmetric, you’ll get more depth by improving dorsiflexion than by hammering hip openers. 

Actionably: test your knee‑to‑wall on both sides, then use split‑squat knee‑over‑toe pulses, slow calf raises with a full stretch, and banded anterior talus glides to expand range, and keep training squats with a small heel lift while you build capacity (per Sato et al. 2012).
candidate.bridge: Your squat is a door: the hips are the door itself, but the ankles are the hinges—if the hinge (dorsiflexion) won’t swing, the door can’t open deep, so you end up bowing forward, popping your heels, or stopping short. A small heel lift is like oiling the hinge so the door glides deeper while you rebuild range.

candidate.topic: Why ankle flexibility predicts squat depth more than hip mobility
candidate.hook: Your deepest squat is decided at your ankles, not your hips—and that’s why all the hip stretching hasn’t moved your depth in months. Fix the ankle hinge, and the bottom finally shows up.
candidate.frame: We’re looking at squat depth through an ankle-first lens: dorsiflexion sets the tibia and torso angles, and the hips follow. When we screen and train the ankle hinge first, your hip work finally has somewhere to go.
candidate.payload: Dorsiflexion is the limiter: it sets how far the knees can travel and thus the tibia angle; to keep your center of mass over mid-foot, the torso must match that angle, so stiff ankles force more forward lean and earlier posterior pelvic tilt, capping depth even if your hips are mobile. When researchers restricted forward knee travel (a proxy for limited dorsiflexion), lifters squatted shallower and shifted torque to the hips with greater trunk inclination (per Fry 2003), while adding a heel lift/weightlifting shoe increased effective dorsiflexion and allowed a more upright torso and deeper knee flexion at the bottom (per Sato 2012). In field screens, weight-bearing lunge (knee-to-wall) dorsiflexion is strongly associated with deep-squat performance and is a more actionable predictor than passive hip ROM for who hits depth (per Rabin 2017), and the test itself is reliable and valid for tracking change (per Powden 2015). Screen ankles first: if your knee-to-wall is limited or asymmetrical, expect hip drills to have diminishing returns until you restore closed-chain dorsiflexion. Train it with bent-knee calf eccentrics, long-duration split-squat knee-over-toe isometrics, and talocrural joint mobilizations, then retest your squat. Once the ankle hinge lets the tibia glide forward, your existing hip mobility finally has somewhere to go—and the bottom shows up.
candidate.bridge: Squatting is like pushing a shopping cart: if the front wheel (your ankle dorsiflexion) is stuck, you end up leaning and muscling it with your torso and hips, and you stall early. Free the wheel—or add a small shim under the heel—and the cart tracks straight to depth.
